name: Color Channel Noise Discrepancy
description: Analyzes and compares the distribution of high-frequency noise across the separated Red, Green, and Blue color channels. Authentic camera sensors possess strict hardware-level Bayer filter physics, naturally causing the Blue and Red channels to be significantly noisier than the Green channel (which has twice as many sensor pixels). AI-generated images lack a physical light sensor, generally outputting a synthesized noise spectrum that is unnaturally uniform or erratically balanced across all three color channels.
algorithm: High-Frequency Spectral Extraction & Channel Variance Comparison
mechanism: The algorithm isolates the R, G, and B channels and applies a high-pass filter (or spatial wavelet transform) to strip away the image content, leaving only the raw 'noise floor'. It then computes the statistical variance of the noise in each channel. In genuine digital photographs, the sensor's Bayer Array allocates 50% of its pixels to Green, and only 25% each to Red and Blue. Because of this photon-gathering disparity, Red and Blue channels are inherently noisier. AI models synthesize noise directly as a digital artifact, generating noise profiles that either treat all RGB channels equally or fail to align with the standard 'Green-dominant SNR' biological sensor constraint.
parameters: Filter: High-pass / Wavelet denoise, Metric: Variance disparity (Var(R) vs Var(G), Var(B) vs Var(G)), Expected ratio: B & R > G
accuracy: High (80-90%) - Highly reliable except on images heavily altered by professional post-processing denoising tools or aggressive cross-platform compression.
source: Chen et al. (2008) / Lukas et al. (2006) - Camera Sensor Pattern Noise Identification
useCase: Distinguishing AI-generated images from authentic photographs by detecting the absence of hardware-induced Bayer array noise imbalances, acting as a virtual hardware inspection.

references.title: Chen, M. et al. (2008). Determining Image Origin and Integrity Using Sensor Noise. IEEE TIFS.
Lukas, J. et al. (2006). Digital Camera Identification from Sensor Pattern Noise. IEEE TIFS.

strengths:
• Relies on a physical fingerprint (Bayer Array physics) that generative AI models do not conceptually understand or mathematically simulate.
• Highly resilient to zero-shot detection against entirely novel architectures (like newer Midjourney or DALL-E versions) due to its purely physical foundation.
• Effective at detecting 'Copy-Move' or spliced image manipulation where the localized channel noise variance suddenly diverges from the rest of the image.
limitations:
• Completely defanged by aggressive noise-reduction software (e.g., Topaz Denoise, Lightroom AI Denoise), which artificially scrubs the authentic sensor noise, triggering a false-positive 'AI' flag.
• Inherently useless on native grayscale or monochrome imagery where color channels have been collapsed or destroyed.
• Heavily compressed social media images (WhatsApp, Facebook) crush high-frequency data, obliterating the delicate noise signatures needed for this analysis.
